title: Group Extensions Complements and Schur Zassenhaus

items.title: Equivalence of group extensions with fixed kernel and fixed quotient
Morphisms of group extensions
In a group extension the kernel is normal and the quotient recovers the base
items.strategy: Unpack short exactness: the image of the injection is the kernel of the quotient map, hence normal, and then apply the first isomorphism theorem to the quotient map.

items.title: A retraction of the kernel in a group extension
A group extension splits exactly when it has a complement or a compatible semidirect-product model, and a kernel retraction forces a direct product
items.strategy: Use the published splitting lemma for the section, complement, and semidirect-product equivalence. Add the retraction criterion by comparing the kernel of a retraction with a complement and conversely constructing a retraction from a complement.

items.title: A complement determines the conjugation action on the kernel
items.strategy: Once the complement is identified with the quotient through the splitting dictionary, transport conjugation by complement elements to an action of the quotient on the kernel.

items.title: A split extension is a direct product exactly when its complement centralizes the kernel
items.strategy: Translate the split extension to a semidirect product by the complement-induced action, and then apply the published criterion that the semidirect product is direct exactly when that action is trivial.

items.title: A group extension induces a well-defined outer action on its kernel
items.strategy: Choose a lift of each quotient element, let it act on the kernel by conjugation, and check that changing the lift alters the automorphism only by an inner automorphism.

items.title: Abstract kernels and the general extension problem
Nonabelian extension obstructions live in H^3 and realized classes form an H^2-torsor
items.strategy: Record the exact Eilenberg-Mac Lane boundary: an abstract kernel may fail to be realizable because of an H^3 obstruction, and when realizable its equivalence classes form a torsor under H^2 of the centre. At authoring this stays citation-only.

items.title: Hall pi-subgroup
A normal Hall subgroup presents the ambient group as an extension of coprime orders
items.strategy: For a normal Hall pi-subgroup N of a finite group G, compare |N| and |G/N| through the Hall-index condition and the quotient-order formula to obtain coprimeness.

items.title: Schur-Zassenhaus existence theorem
items.strategy: Induct on the finite group order with a normal Hall subgroup N. Reduce through proper normal overgroups or minimal normal subgroups, handle the elementary-abelian coprime-action step explicitly, and rebuild the complement in the ambient group.

items.title: Schur-Zassenhaus conjugacy when the kernel or quotient is solvable
items.strategy: Follow the classical induction: compare two complements through suitable normal subgroups, pass to smaller quotient or subgroup instances under the solvability hypothesis, and lift the resulting conjugations back to the ambient group.

items.title: The full Schur-Zassenhaus conjugacy theorem
items.strategy: Record the clean finite-group statement that complements to a normal Hall subgroup are always conjugate. At authoring this is source-cited and proved_here=false unless the proof is deliberately expanded beyond the classical solvable-boundary route.

items.title: Extensions with coprime kernel and quotient split
items.strategy: A finite extension with coprime kernel and quotient orders has a normal Hall kernel, so Schur-Zassenhaus produces a complement and the splitting dictionary converts that complement into a split extension.

items.title: Complete group
If the kernel is complete, the extension splits over its centralizer
items.strategy: A complete kernel has trivial centre and trivial outer action, so the quotient action lifts uniquely to genuine conjugation. The centralizer of the kernel then has trivial intersection with the kernel and maps isomorphically onto the quotient, yielding the split complement.

items.title: FALSE: a set-theoretic section of an extension is automatically a homomorphism
items.strategy: Refute by choosing a quotient map with an obvious set section whose square fails the homomorphism law upstairs.

items.title: FALSE: isomorphic middle groups force equivalent extensions with fixed kernel and quotient
items.strategy: Refute by exhibiting two extension structures on the same abstract group whose kernels and quotient maps cannot be matched by an isomorphism fixing the named kernel and quotient identifications.

items.title: FALSE: every split group extension is a direct product
items.strategy: Refute with a split semidirect product whose complement acts nontrivially on the kernel.

items.title: FALSE: Schur-Zassenhaus says every Hall subgroup is normal
items.strategy: Refute by separating the theorem's actual hypothesis of a normal Hall subgroup from the existence of arbitrary Hall subgroups.

items.title: FALSE: Schur-Zassenhaus conjugacy needs no solvability or deeper input
items.strategy: Refute by distinguishing the classical solvable-boundary proof carried locally from the stronger clean theorem that uses deeper finite-group input in the chosen source.

title: Group Extensions Complements and Schur Zassenhaus — Examples

items.title: A set-theoretic section of C_4 onto C_2 need not be a homomorphism
items.strategy: Take the quotient map C_4 to C_2 and choose the set section sending the nontrivial class to a generator of C_4. Its square is nontrivial upstairs although the image square is trivial downstairs.

items.title: The dihedral group of order eight is a split extension of C_4 by C_2
items.strategy: Use the inversion action of C_2 on C_4 to realize D_8 as a semidirect product, identify the rotation subgroup as the kernel and a reflection subgroup as a complement, and read off the split exact sequence.

items.title: The split extension C_2 × C_2 of C_2 by C_2 is direct
items.strategy: Write the group as an external direct product, use the two coordinate subgroups as kernel and complement, and verify that they centralize each other so the split extension is not merely semidirect.

items.title: A_4 has four complements to its normal Klein four subgroup
items.strategy: List the normal Klein four subgroup of A_4 and its four order-three subgroups, then verify directly that each order-three subgroup is a complement and that Schur-Zassenhaus explains why they lie in one conjugacy class.

items.title: The three transposition subgroups of S_3 are conjugate complements to A_3
items.strategy: Use A_3 as the normal Hall subgroup of S_3, identify the order-two subgroups as complements, and then compare them both by direct conjugation and by the Schur-Zassenhaus conjugacy theorem.

items.title: The cyclic group Z/9 supports inequivalent extensions of C_3 by C_3
items.strategy: Put two extension structures on the same Klein four group by choosing different kernels and quotient maps, and show that no automorphism fixing the named C_2 kernel and quotient identifications carries one structure to the other.

title: Crossed Homomorphisms Complements and First Cohomology

items.title: Crossed homomorphism for a G-group
With abelian coefficients, crossed homomorphisms form an abelian group
items.strategy: Use pointwise multiplication in multiplicative notation, or pointwise addition in additive notation, and check the crossed-homomorphism identity termwise.

items.title: Principal crossed homomorphism for abelian coefficients
Principal crossed homomorphisms form a subgroup
items.strategy: Compute the sum and inverse of principal crossed homomorphisms using the abelian coefficient law and the action identities.

items.title: First cohomology via crossed homomorphisms
First group cohomology via inhomogeneous one-cocycles
The inhomogeneous one-cocycle model agrees with crossed homomorphisms in degree one
items.strategy: Write the degree-one inhomogeneous differential explicitly, identify its cocycle equation with the crossed-homomorphism identity, identify its coboundaries with the principal crossed homomorphisms, and conclude that the two quotient constructions coincide.

items.title: For a trivial action, first cohomology is Hom
items.strategy: Under the trivial action the crossed-homomorphism equation becomes the ordinary homomorphism law, and the principal crossed homomorphisms vanish.

items.title: For a finite group, uniquely divisible coefficients have trivial first cohomology
items.strategy: Average a crossed homomorphism over the finite group, divide by the group order in the uniquely divisible coefficient group, and verify that the original cocycle is the resulting principal crossed homomorphism.

items.title: The graph subgroup attached to a map into a semidirect product
A graph subgroup is a complement exactly for a crossed homomorphism
items.strategy: Multiply two graph elements in the semidirect product and compare with the graph of the product in the quotient. The graph is closed exactly when the crossed-homomorphism identity holds, and the projection to G is then an isomorphism onto a complement.

items.title: Kernel conjugation by an element of the coefficient group corresponds to a principal crossed homomorphism
items.strategy: Conjugate the graph subgroup by a kernel element inside the semidirect product and compute the new graph function explicitly; the difference from the old one is exactly the principal crossed homomorphism determined by that element.

items.title: First cohomology classifies complements up to kernel conjugacy
items.strategy: Send a cocycle to its graph complement in the semidirect product and send a complement back to its graph function. The previous lemmas identify exactly when two such complements differ by kernel conjugation, so the resulting bijection is H^1.

items.title: First nonabelian cohomology as a pointed set
Nonabelian first cohomology classifies complements as a pointed set
items.strategy: Repeat the graph-subgroup correspondence for a general G-group M in M ⋊ G. The orbit relation now comes from conjugation by M itself, so the classification is a pointed set rather than a quotient group.

items.title: Restriction, inflation, and the quotient conjugation action on first cohomology
Inflation-restriction exact sequence in degree one
items.strategy: Write inflation and restriction on cocycles explicitly. Injectivity of inflation, vanishing of the composite, and the middle exactness all follow by modifying a cocycle by a principal one so that it vanishes on the normal subgroup and then descends to the quotient.

items.title: FALSE: every crossed homomorphism is an ordinary homomorphism
items.strategy: Refute with a nontrivial action where the crossed-homomorphism equation visibly differs from the ordinary homomorphism law.

items.title: FALSE: first cohomology with nonabelian coefficients is a group
items.strategy: Refute by exhibiting a nonabelian coefficient group whose complement classes carry only a distinguished basepoint and no natural binary operation.

items.title: FALSE: first cohomology classifies all subgroups of a semidirect product
items.strategy: Refute by separating complements, which project isomorphically onto the quotient, from arbitrary subgroups of the semidirect product.

items.title: FALSE: whole-semiproduct conjugacy is the equivalence relation behind first cohomology
items.strategy: Refute by showing that the quotient H^1 remembers kernel conjugacy classes of complements, not arbitrary conjugacy inside the whole semidirect product.

items.title: FALSE: the cochain and crossed-homomorphism definitions of first cohomology agree automatically
items.strategy: Refute by noting that the degree-one differential and sign convention must be written out and checked before the cocycle and coboundary formulas can be identified.

title: Crossed Homomorphisms Complements and First Cohomology — Examples

items.title: With trivial action, H^1(C_2,C_3) is zero
items.strategy: Apply the trivial-action identification H^1=Hom and note that every homomorphism from a group of order two to a group of order three is trivial.

items.title: Crossed homomorphisms from a cyclic group are determined by the value on a generator
items.strategy: Let t generate the cyclic group and iterate the crossed-homomorphism identity to express the value on every power of t in terms of the value at t and the given action.

items.title: The affine group AGL(1,p) has one kernel-conjugacy class of complements to its translation subgroup
items.strategy: View AGL(1,p) as F_p ⋊ F_p^×, use the coprime-order vanishing theorem to see H^1(F_p^×,F_p)=0, and conclude that every complement to the translation subgroup is conjugate by a translation.

items.title: Kernel-conjugate complements differ by a principal crossed homomorphism
items.strategy: Inside an explicit semidirect product, compute two complements whose graph functions differ by conjugation with a chosen kernel element and match that difference with the corresponding principal crossed homomorphism.

items.title: With trivial C_2-action on S_3, the nonabelian H^1 pointed set has two classes
items.strategy: For the trivial action, nonabelian 1-cocycles are homomorphisms C_2 to S_3. Up to conjugacy there are the trivial map and the class of a transposition, giving a two-point pointed set with no natural group law.

items.title: The inversion crossed homomorphism C_2 → Z is not an ordinary homomorphism
items.strategy: Let the nontrivial element of C_2 act on Z by negation and send it to 1. The crossed-homomorphism identity holds, but an ordinary homomorphism from C_2 to Z would have to be trivial.
